rv.q: English eccentricity at its madcap best.
It’s that kind of show, with nothing new to say about our Victorian past (far less the present), and lots of funny ways of saying it.
Yet despite Leslie’s boisterous direction, Evans’ satiric flair and a thoroughly entertaining ensemble, this is a long haul.
Heavens, though, without more to motor it than parody, with takedowns of Victorian prejudice and repression that are affable yet predictable, this feels like well-trodden terrain.
Part of the problem is it gives off this constant sense of trying to be funny rather than being funny.
But mostly it chunters on at a level of profound mediocrity.

The clichéd characters are either whimsically naive or downright villainous and each member of the cast plays to the ludicrousness in Mark Evans’ script, grabbing every one of the multitudinous opportunities to ham it up with joyous aplomb.
But the show unwittingly perpetuates the prejudice it seeks to disparage.
The pace of Caroline Leslie’s production is hectic and the shouting sometimes excessive.
There is lots to enjoy here; the constant silliness means there nothing serious in the show, but that is exactly the point.
[The play's] tropes ... get stretched to the point of translucence, and it all lacks a little cohesion. It’s like feasting on canapes – periodically delightful, but not exactly filling.
The performances lift a tired and shtick-filled script but likely by nowhere near enough to satisfy an audience paying West End seat prices for a show with a big celebrity name.
Even comic exaggeration wears out its welcome if it isn’t anchored in some kind of truth.
A fusion of farce, panto-type jokes, physical comedy, all with a bit of Dickens, Brief Expectations is ingenious and hilarious in equal measure, a must-see for a great night out.
I came out of the theatre feeling refreshed, joyous and far from bleak.
Bleak Expectations still offers a wild farcical romp into the world of Dickens perfect for anyone who enjoys a laid-back style of comedy.
Its inoffensive silliness is enough to put a smile on the face of all but the most demanding theatregoer.

Often very funny but showing signs of strain in its change of mediums, Bleak Expectations still managed to provide an enjoyable evening at the theatre, and often had me thinking it was completely stupid – a compliment, with this kind of show.
A hilariously light comedy about a questionable era that remains questionable no matter how much fun we make of it.
Whilst the concept is great, the show is more amusing than riotously funny, and the absence of great comedy means the lack of plot is only highlighted.

cn.t: This Dickensian parody divides critics with its silly, pun-filled humor and celebrity narrators. Some praise its intelligent wit and energetic cast, while others find it overlong and stretched thin at two hours.

vr.q: I found I'd enjoyed my evening, but I was not thinking, 'Please, sir, may I have some more.'
